title: Flydubai Co-Pilot Confesses Gaza Revenge Motive, Had Planned Ben Gurion Crash
excerpt: Hamam al-Hammami told investigators he sought an airline job to carry out the attack and wanted to die a martyr; investigators are now probing whether he acted alone, while Captain Smit Machchhar recovers from a fractured skull.
body:
• Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami told investigators he tried to bring down Flydubai Flight FZ1073 "in revenge for Gaza" and wanted to die as a martyr, according to Israeli media reports citing interrogation findings.
  • Investigators say the attack was planned long before he joined Flydubai: he allegedly sought jobs at multiple airlines, chose Flydubai because it flies to Tel Aviv, and intended to crash the plane into Ben Gurion Airport — with a US military base in Jordan as a backup target.
  • Israel's Shin Bet is now involved in the investigation; officials are examining al-Hammami's trips to countries hostile to Israel to determine whether he acted alone or was recruited. No evidence of outside direction has been made public.
  • Meanwhile, the Indian embassy in the UAE said Captain Smit Machchhar — the Indian pilot who fought off the attack — is "making steady progress, regaining health" after emergency surgery.

The Omani co-pilot accused of trying to bring down Flydubai Flight FZ1073 told investigators he acted "in revenge for Gaza" and wanted to die as a martyr, according to new details from the interrogation reported by Israel's Channel 12 — the first clear account of the motive behind the September 30 cockpit attack that left the Indian captain fighting for his life.

The confession

"I did it as revenge for Gaza. I wanted to die as a shahid," Hamam al-Hammami reportedly told investigators during questioning in the United Arab Emirates, where he is in custody. The reported statement has not been independently verified by wire services, and investigators have not publicly released a full interrogation transcript — but the account fits what passengers witnessed after they overpowered him: the subdued co-pilot repeatedly begged the Israelis restraining him to kill him, crying "Kill me! Kill me!" in English, over and over.

https://x.com/firstpost/status/2107365690730840504

According to a transcript of the interrogation provided to The Jerusalem Post by an Israeli intelligence source, al-Hammami said: "I tried to get hired by all the airlines. I planned the operation even before I was accepted by the company. The dream was to crash into Ben Gurion Airport." A Saudi official briefed on the interrogation told The Wall Street Journal that al-Hammami acknowledged his intention to deliberately crash the aircraft and said he was "not afraid of death."

A long-planned attack

If investigators' accounts are confirmed, the case goes well beyond an impulsive cockpit assault. Officials cited by Israeli media believe al-Hammami deliberately chose Flydubai because it operates flights to Tel Aviv. His alleged plan: dispose of the captain, continue Flight 1073 normally to receive landing clearances, then crash into a building or aircraft at Ben Gurion Airport. He reportedly waited until the aircraft was over Jordan to seize the cockpit, to avoid raising alarms.

There was also a backup target: if the flight could not reach Israel, he allegedly intended to crash into a US military installation in Jordan. Investigators believe he had considered carrying out the attack as early as July 2026 but abandoned that attempt because a friend was among the crew.

The Wall Street Journal reported on October 5 that Flydubai had performed a criminal-background check when hiring al-Hammami but did not contact Oman to vet his experience — and that he had flown to Israel on multiple occasions. Earlier reporting indicated he had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns about extremist views and placed in a deradicalisation programme — red flags that investigators are now examining to see how they were handled and whether information was adequately shared between aviation and security authorities.

"I did it as revenge for Gaza. I wanted to die as a shahid."

— Hamam al-Hammami, as reported by Israel's Channel 12, citing investigators

Alone or directed?

The critical open question is whether al-Hammami acted alone. Israel's military censor cleared for publication on Monday evening that the Shin Bet is directly involved in the investigation. A Mossad representative briefed ministers at a security cabinet meeting on Sunday, saying investigators had discovered that "in recent years the terrorist visited countries hostile to Israel, some of them enemy states," and that authorities are investigating whether "during these visits someone or some organization activated or recruited him." No evidence establishing that another country or organization directed the attack has yet been made public.

US President Donald Trump said Monday that he personally believes Iran was behind the attack. "I do. I personally do," he told a reporter — without providing evidence. The UAE has officially classified the incident as a terrorist act.

Captain Machchhar recovering

Amid the grim revelations, there was better news about the man who stopped the attack. The Indian embassy in the UAE said Captain Smit Machchhar — the Indian pilot who fought off al-Hammami's assault with an emergency axe in the cockpit — is "making steady progress, regaining health" after undergoing emergency surgery for a fractured skull. The Dubai Crown Prince visited him in hospital, and Israel's prime minister called him a "true hero" and invited him to Israel.

What's next

Investigators in the UAE and Saudi Arabia continue to examine al-Hammami's communications, contacts and travel, with his cellphone a major focus. The aviation industry faces hard questions about how a man flagged by his own country's authorities ended up in a commercial cockpit on an Israel-bound flight — and whether the industry's vetting systems need a fundamental overhaul.
image_caption: A Flydubai Boeing 737-800. Co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami allegedly planned to crash Flight FZ1073 into Ben Gurion Airport in revenge for Gaza.
nri_angle: An Indian pilot's heroism saved Flight FZ1073, and his recovery continues; the case also spotlights aviation-security gaps that matter to the millions of Indians who fly Gulf routes every year.
